pos.personaBrief: Viv Anderson says Clough wanted football played 'on the floor', and the team passed its way through games, but nothing in the evidence shows a possession-count obsession; the 1980 final was held on with Clough admitting they hung on.

pro.personaBrief: Simple passing football on the floor with forwards who hold the ball up until midfield support arrives (Wilson via WSC), and Viv Anderson's 'pass to him' instruction; no frantic verticality is documented.

est.personaBrief: Clough fixed roles for each player and disliked blackboard diagrams (WSC); the flexible 4-3-3 had Robertson wide and each man knowing his job, not rondo-style relational play.

lar.personaBrief: The 1977/78 4-3-3 relied on Robertson's crosses for Woodcock and Withe, and Francis spent much time on the wing (WSC), though the 1980 final used five in midfield.

blo.personaBrief: No source shows pressing; O'Neill says things were built around hurting the opposition and McGovern says tactics rarely changed, with a pragmatic, compact back four (FourFourTwo).

mar.personaBrief: Evidence is thin; Clough rarely discussed opponents (O'Neill) and gave fixed jobs to each player, which reads as clear personal responsibility without a dedicated star-marking scheme.

pla.personaBrief: McGovern: 'we never changed the tactics much under Brian'; O'Neill says he seldom spoke about opponents; Forest kept its identity built on the players he found and selected for their roles.

res.personaBrief: Clough wanted to win everything ('piss all over them') while insisting on passing football; the team was called unadventurous in 1977, and in 1980 it held on to win the final.

sis.personaBrief: Clough picked players to fit fixed roles and relied on concise instructions (WSC), with no tactics but men who knew their jobs; stars were not licensed to roam.

jog.personaBrief: He bought tough competitors like Burns, Lloyd and Mackay-type men yet wanted the ball passed on the floor; roles required hold-up and winning duels alongside technique.

bas.personaBrief: Clough bought experienced players (Clark, Barrett, Lloyd, Shilton) to help the young lads (Viv Anderson) and built championships mainly by signings plus few existing youngsters.

lid.personaBrief: He ruled by fear and unpredictability, ordering expensive signings to fetch balls from nettles and refusing even the chairman entry (WSC, FourFourTwo, Set Pieces).
